raw_text:
# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

### Introduction
The clinical translation of bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) in percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) represents one of the most intriguing chapters in interventional cardiology. The journey began with the Igaki-Tamai stent, a non-drug-eluting, poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) scaffold that demonstrated long-term safety and feasibility [1]. This milestone paved the way for the first-generation everolimus-eluting Absorb BVS (Abbott Vascular), initially evaluated in the ABSORB Cohort A [2] and Cohort B [3] trials, which reported progressive bioresorption and the return of physiological vasomotion. The second-generation design of this platform was further validated in early clinical testing [4].

### Pivotal Randomized Trials and Safety Setbacks
However, larger randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing the first-generation Absorb BVS against contemporary metallic cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents (CoCr-EES) revealed significant safety limitations. The three-year outcomes of the ABSORB II trial raised alarms by showing a higher rate of late target lesion failure (TLF) [5]. This was followed by the landmark ABSORB III trial, which showed that while BVS was non-inferior to CoCr-EES at one year [6], BVS-treated patients suffered from significantly higher rates of target vessel-related myocardial infarction (TV-MI) and device thrombosis at three years [7], which persisted through five years of follow-up [8]. The ABSORB IV trial, designed to evaluate the scaffold in a broader, less complex patient cohort using an optimized implantation technique, still demonstrated higher rates of TLF over long-term follow-up [9,10]. 

Furthermore, the investigator-initiated AIDA trial, which evaluated the Absorb BVS in routine, real-world PCI clinical practice, was halted early due to a nearly threefold increase in scaffold thrombosis [11]. Extensive meta-analyses of pooled individual patient data confirmed these safety concerns, showing elevated risks of scaffold thrombosis and target vessel-related adverse events at two years [12], three years [13], and five years [14]. Similarly, real-world outcomes from registries such as GHOST-EU highlighted high rates of early and midterm scaffold thrombosis [15].

### Mechanistic Insights and the "PSP" Implantation Protocol
Detailed analysis of clinical failures identified critical biomechanical and procedural factors. Investigations into scaffold thrombosis demonstrated that early events were primarily driven by mechanical issues like underexpansion and malapposition [16]. Conversely, very late scaffold thrombosis was frequently associated with late-acquired strut malapposition, uncovered struts, and scaffold dismantling or discontinuity during the bioresorption process [17]. To address these limitations, experts developed the "PSP" strategy: aggressive Pre-dilation, accurate Sizing of the vessel, and high-pressure Post-dilation with non-compliant balloons [18]. Post-hoc analyses of the ABSORB trials confirmed that strict adherence to the PSP technique significantly reduced the incidence of target lesion failure and scaffold thrombosis [19].

### Guidelines, Next-Generation Platforms, and Future Directions
Based on the safety concerns of first-generation polymeric devices, the 2018 ESC/EACTS guidelines issued a Class III (harm) recommendation, stating that bioresorbable polymeric scaffolds should not be used in routine clinical practice [20]. An expert consensus panel emphasized that if BVS are utilized, meticulous lesion preparation and mandatory intravascular imaging guidance are essential [21]. 

To overcome the challenges of PLLA-based polymeric devices, newer platforms have emerged. The second-generation drug-eluting absorbable metal scaffold (DREAMS-2G, commercially Magmaris) demonstrated acceptable safety and performance in the BIOSOLVE-II trial [22]. It was further validated in the large BIOSOLVE-IV registry, showing a favorable safety profile with low rates of scaffold thrombosis [23]. More recently, the third-generation magnesium-based scaffold (DREAMS-3G, Freesolve) demonstrated encouraging one-year clinical and imaging results in the BIOMAG-I trial [24].

Simultaneously, next-generation polymeric BVS with thinner struts and novel polymers are under evaluation. These include the Fantom scaffold, a tyrosine-derived polycarbonate platform evaluated in the FANTOM II trial [25]; the MeRes100 thin-strut polymeric scaffold [26]; the Mirage microfiber scaffold [27]; and the DESolve novolimus-eluting scaffold [28]. To progress, these new platforms must be benchmarked against standard metallic DES, such as those evaluated in the SPIRIT IV trial [29], and must routinely utilize intravascular imaging to guide scaffold expansion, as validated by trials such as ILUMIEN III [30].
